items.explain: They have the chest X-ray eventually, but late, after refusing to be escorted by a support worker.
They begin treatment for a suspected lung infection, with medicine handed out under supervision at the shelter where a bed is held.
The people who share shelters and nights outdoors with them are flagged to be tested for infection too.
They stop the treatment partway and lose touch with doctors, partly because they have no address to be contacted at.

items.plain: Fails to get back into work
items.explain: They try to find a job or open a bank account without an address, but it fails; old warehouse jobs are gone.
They die by the river from a long-untreated lung illness, made worse by cold and not enough food.
They are expected to die in 2055, aged 49, from a lung infection that never got treated.
They collect blood pressure medicine and get checked at the library, keeping it partly under control as long as they keep visiting daily.

items.plain: Gets a reliable winter shelter bed
items.explain: They get a standing shelter bed for winter, so they sleep outside less, though still on some nights.
They are tested after spending months near someone with a suspected lung infection, and may still carry a hidden infection.
Their friends move away, are kept apart, or withdraw, leaving only library staff and a distant sibling to talk to.
When medicine or a bed slips, their blood pressure spikes dangerously; they spend a short time in hospital, then return to the shelter.
Worn down by years of near-street living and poor food, they have a fatal stroke at a shelter or library.
They are expected to die of a stroke in 2060, aged 75.
The mould in their flat is cleaned up quickly and the complaint is closed, ending outside questions about it.
An automatic report to child services is closed without action; they never learn it existed, and their worry about losing their child eases.
Their child wheezes less once the damp is gone, needs fewer clinic visits, and goes to school more regularly.
They keep an insecure care job with unpaid travel, stay on antidepressants long-term, and their low mood is managed, not cured.
They look for steadier hours or a senior care role as their child starts secondary school, but success is unclear.
Years of lifting people in care work leave them with lasting physical pain, so they stop working early and go on disability benefits.
They ignore official warnings and return to the council building with a friend to keep pushing for the tenants' group.
With no income to take fines from, their unpaid fines and council tax go to bailiffs and grow with extra charges.
If they withhold charges, the council takes them to court over arrears on their home, and they attend and fight it.
Members leave after rumours about their past debts spread, leaving only a few, so they go back to campaigning alone.
They stay out of official work and benefits, possibly getting by on cash delivery or driving jobs.
They may suffer a heart-related health crisis or growing difficulty walking, while living on a fifth floor with an often-broken lift.
They keep getting agency shifts at the warehouse, earning some declared wages instead of only cash, for now.
A check on their cash deposits ends without penalty, and their informal friends and contacts drift away.
Machines take over the warehouse, their shifts dwindle below what they need to live on, as happened before.
They go back to earning cash informally, sometimes stay out overnight, fall behind on phone bills and pawn belongings.
They leave the city for warehouse jobs in a nearby town and drop out of the system's view.
They keep low-paid cash work at the scrapyard all winter, giving their day a routine that fits their medicine pickups.
A background check flag is cleared, so they can start supervised volunteering at the library if they don't pull out.
They meet their child and grandchild for a second Christmas, as long as their drug tests stay clean.
Police keep searching them because of their record, finding nothing, which adds stress and risk of relapse.
They see their grandchild regularly and stay on long-term methadone rather than quitting entirely.
As their body weakens in their sixties, casual work ends and they live on benefits in their flat.
They die around age 72 from heart and lung strain after decades of opioid use.

items.plain: Dies of heart and lung failure
items.explain: They are expected to die in 2066, aged 72, when the heart and lungs give out.
They pick up antidepressants only at the clinic each Tuesday with a neighbour, at the late spouse's old appointment time.
A young helper who also collected their medicine moves away to university, leaving just one person helping.
They update their will themselves without a lawyer, a common step when preparing for death.
They may fall or collapse at home and lie there over a day before anyone finds them.
The neighbour who goes with them to collect medicine starts missing visits due to home troubles.
They may quietly stop their medication and stop going to the clinic, despite reminder calls.
Living alone in old age after losing a spouse, their heart weakens and they keep losing weight; home care is offered.
They are expected to die in 2057, aged 88, from heart failure and frailty.
They may try taking concerns about the council's housing algorithm to outside appeals or journalists, though less likely after being refused.
Their engagement is called off; new evening and weekend shifts cut time together and contact with supportive colleagues.
They file an official complaint after a public meeting fails to answer their questions, delayed by polite, empty replies.
They may leave for a library job elsewhere, though fixed work commitments and refused leave make interviews hard.
If they stay, they lead a local memory project, keep private notes offline, and stop asking questions publicly.
They may be diagnosed with long-term high blood pressure from stress, working evenings and weekends and living alone.
